question: A browser shows "connection refused" for `api.example.com`. Which layer failed?
options: HTTP: the server answered with a 404
TCP: no program accepted a connection on that address and port, so no HTTP request was ever sent
DNS: the name has no TTL
TLS: the response body was not JSON
explanation: A refused connection happens at the TCP level, before any HTTP request or status code exists. A 404 needs a working connection and a server that read the request.

question: A client times out while waiting for the answer to `PUT /profiles/7`. Is it safe to send the same request again?
options: Yes: PUT replaces the resource, so applying it twice leaves the same state as applying it once (it is idempotent)
No: PUT always creates a new resource
Only if the server returned 500
No: HTTP forbids retries
explanation: PUT is idempotent: it sets the resource to the given state, so a repeated request ends in the same state. A repeated POST may create a second resource.

question: The path `/notes` supports GET and POST. A client sends `DELETE /notes`. Which status code fits best?
options: 200 OK with an error message in the body
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
405 Method Not Allowed: the resource exists but not with this method
explanation: 405 tells the client the path is valid and the method is not, which is different from a resource that does not exist (404). The client made the mistake, so it is a 4xx, not a 5xx.

question: An API answers invalid input with `200 OK` and `{ "error": "title is required" }`. What is the practical problem?
options: JSON cannot carry error messages
Browsers reject 200 responses with a body
Clients, caches and monitoring read the status code, so they treat the failure as a success
TCP retransmits 200 responses forever
explanation: Status codes are read by machines without parsing the body: retry policies, caches and error-rate alerts all see success. A 400 Bad Request states the outcome where every tool looks.

question: Why should the server validate a price even when the web client already checks it?
options: Clients run on devices you do not control and can send any request, so the server is the only place a rule is enforced
Browsers cannot run validation code
HTTP removes the body of POST requests
DNS may change the price on the way
explanation: Anyone can modify a client or call the API directly with a tool. Client-side checks improve the experience; server-side checks are the actual rule.

question: A team moves its API to a new IP address and updates DNS. Some users still reach the old server for a while. Why?
options: TCP keeps the old address in the HTTP headers
Status code 301 is cached by every server
The old server forwards requests forever
Resolvers and clients cache DNS answers until their time-to-live expires
explanation: DNS answers are cached for their TTL at many layers (resolvers, operating systems, browsers). A lower TTL before a migration shortens the time clients keep the old address.
